passage:
Monday. In the product team's planning meeting, eight voices argued about the new sign-up screen. Varun, the only designer working from Guwahati, joined by video, unmuted twice and was talked over both times. Avni, the team lead, noticed his square go dark when he switched his camera off.
Wednesday. Avni opened the follow-up meeting differently. "Before anyone else speaks: Varun, you've tested this with users in the north-east. What did you see?" A pause. Then Varun shared his screen. People on slow networks were quitting at the photo-upload step. Nobody in the Bengaluru office had seen that.
Friday. The team dropped the photo step. At the all-hands, Avni put up a slide: "Fewer drop-offs. Idea: Varun." Later he messaged her, "First time I've felt properly on this team." The next Monday, he unmuted without being asked.

qa.q: At which step were people on slow networks quitting?
What was Varun feeling when he switched his camera off on Monday?
qa.a: He probably felt unheard and left out after being talked over twice.

qa.q: Which of Avni's choices changed things, and why?
qa.a: She asked Varun to speak first, before the louder voices, then credited him by name at the all-hands, so his knowledge shaped the decision and he felt he belonged.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team see the Friday slide?
qa.a: They may realise they had missed something important by talking over Varun, and that hearing quieter members makes decisions better.

grounding: Shows a team lead from the majority giving a quiet, remote member real airtime and credit, improving the decision and his belonging.
